free_tier.stated: A free tier exists and is funded by forum activity: '€ 0 dauerhaft' with 'nur mit Free MB-Guthaben' (only with free-MB credit), and free users unlock premium hosters only from 5,000 free MB.
free_tier.notes: Free users are charged the whole file size in advance; premium users are charged actual bytes times a per-host factor.

per_object_cap.stated: Not published; the metered unit is the download itself, and a free download is charged at full size before it starts.

retention.stated: Traffic expires with the package: unused volume is lost unless the free 'Keep' option moves it into a new package of the same tier before expiry.

egress.terms: Every download spends package traffic at a per-host factor: 'Premiumnutzern wird nur der tatsächlich verbrauchte Traffic multipliziert mit den Faktoren ... berechnet', so one host can cost 33%, 50% or 100% of its size and another more than 100%.
egress.free_allowance: free-MB credit earned on the forum, plus a monthly volume bought with the package

interface_detail: A documented JSON endpoint at https://high-way.me/load.php?json&link=... plus login and traffic calls; the API is German-language and the error text is inside an 'error' tag.
tooling: JDownloader and a community API wrapper; no rclone backend found; the site is German-only
chaining: A German-language market with its own hoster contracts; the only service here that bills by host-specific multipliers, so its per-terabyte cost depends on which hosts a user uses.

reliability_note: Every download debits package traffic at a host factor and a free download is charged in full before it starts; a Cloudhoster blocking HIGHWAY's account or server IPs is an expected event the terms describe; the API's German error strings are the only diagnostic.

notes: Candidates for the first failure: traffic exhaustion (error 3), the per-host traffic ceiling (14/15), or a hoster blocking HIGHWAY (code 11). the per-host ceiling is the one a single large release meets. The API documentation is a 2015 forum post; it is the vendor's own and the only one published, and the last changelog entry read is from 2016. This record corrects the ip-class lane's classification. Its table lists High-Way under 'server IPs at registration (reported)' and gives the verdict fails-egress, and its own prose then says High-Way 'gates the registration instead of the download' - which is the refusal of a class at signup, not a download-time class rule. The headline claim 'the other six refuse the class' counts High-Way as one of the six. Its own documentation refuses nothing; the gate is manual vetting, which is an identity constraint. The records that already existed each priced one line of this page and neither normalised TB to TiB, so the EUR 12.00 30-day rate and the EUR 32.50 no-expiry rate were both being compared against per-TiB figures from other lanes and each was 10% better than it is. This record carries the whole grid and the TiB normalisation. The floor is the annual 9 TB package, not the 30-day 1 TB one: EUR 8.33 per TB-month against EUR 12.00 is a 31% cut for a 12-month commitment, and the 12 TB annual (EUR 110) is worse per byte than the 9 TB annual (EUR 75), which is the one non-monotonic rung in the ladder. The 'ab' prices are floors, not prices: EUR 3.99 buys the smallest Premium package and the tariff a user would actually need is the byte package. The best price per TB and the only one whose currency does not rot, at the cost of a reviewed registration and a German-only contract. Fetched files are still not stored. Abandonment condition: if the 2038 sunset is brought forward, the indefinite claim shrinks. The cheapest-looking number on the page is the wrong one: EUR 3.99 buys the plan, not traffic, and every downloaded byte is charged again through a package. Free MB can be bought, so the 'free' tier is a credit scheme, not an allowance. Ranked here on mechanism rather than numbers: the factor system is real and documented, but nothing about the caps is observable without an approved account.
